definition: A data center is a physical room, building, or facility for storing, managing, and disseminating data and information, including computer systems and associated components, housing IT infrastructure, and training artificial intelligence.
details: The Energy Independence and Security Act of 2007 defines a data center as "any facility that primarily contains electronic equipment used to process, store, and transmit digital information." This includes "a free-standing structure" or "a facility within a larger structure, that uses environmental control equipment to maintain the proper conditions for the operation of electronic equipment." According to IBM, data centers date back to the 1940s, with the U.S. military's Electrical Numerical Integrator and Computer (ENIAC) as an early example. Data centers have different models depending on their workloads. An enterprise (on-premises) model hosts IT infrastructure and data on-premises, while cloud data centers, including hyperscale data centers, house IT infrastructure resources through an internet connection used by cloud service providers such as Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud Platform, IBM Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. They frequently contain thousands of servers and many miles of high-speed data connection equipment, with the largest occupying up to 10,000,000 sq ft (930,000 m2). explainer.lead: A data center is the physical home of digital computing: a facility housing the equipment that processes, stores, and transmits information. These facilities make cloud services, AI training, and many everyday online applications possible, while their growing demand for electricity and water has become an important concern.

tiers.eli5: A data center is like a huge, carefully air-conditioned library, except its shelves hold computers and its books are digital information. When you use an online app, computers in one of these buildings may store your files, work out an answer, and send it back. Some are enormous cloud facilities, while smaller edge facilities sit closer to users so answers can arrive faster.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use enterprise, managed-service, colocation, cloud or hyperscale, and edge facilities according to workload, ownership, scale, and latency requirements. A team might operate its own servers in leased colocation space, consume cloud infrastructure from a hyperscale provider, or place edge capacity near users and data sources. Power and cooling capacity, high-speed connectivity, and energy and water use are central constraints, and the facility categories can overlap rather than forming a strict taxonomy.
tiers.paperLevel: The Energy Independence and Security Act of 2007 defines a data center as any facility that primarily contains electronic equipment used to process, store, and transmit digital information, including a freestanding structure or an environmentally controlled facility within a larger structure. Classifications by ownership, scale, and intended use are not mutually exclusive. The International Energy Agency estimated consumption of about 415 TWh, or roughly 1.5% of global electricity, in 2024 and projects about 945 TWh by 2030.

explainer.example: A company rents space in an Equinix colocation data center instead of constructing its own facility. The center provides shared space, power, and cooling, while the company supplies and manages its own computing components; its applications then communicate with users over network connections.

explainer.intuition: Instead of every organization keeping all its computers in a back room, computing equipment can be concentrated in facilities designed to power, cool, connect, and operate it reliably. The facility may serve one organization, many tenants, a cloud provider's customers, or users nearby.
howItWorks: House servers and associated electronic equipment in a room, building, or facility.
Provide power, cooling, and environmental controls for the equipment.
Connect the equipment with high-speed data links to users and networks.
Process, store, and transmit digital information for applications and AI workloads.
Use an enterprise, managed, colocation, hyperscale, or edge model as needed.
explainer.whyItMatters: Data centers provide the physical capacity behind cloud computing, internet connectivity, large-scale data processing, and AI training. Their expansion also brings major economic effects alongside concerns about electricity and water consumption, increased electricity costs, and local opposition to new projects.
misconceptions: A data center is not just a collection of servers; it also requires power, cooling, connectivity, and environmental controls.
The cloud is not placeless: cloud providers deliver their services from physical data centers.
Edge facilities are not miniature hyperscale campuses; they are deliberately distributed near users or data sources to reduce latency.
Enterprise, colocation, hyperscale, and edge classifications can overlap.
